title: Portuguese grammar
about: From your very first conversation to everyday talk with Brazilians, one short lesson at a time. Each lesson gives you something you can say straight away, then the grammar that makes it work. You don't need to know any grammar: each grammar word is explained when you first need it. Every example is Brazilian Portuguese as people really speak it, with você for “you”; where everyday speech and careful writing differ, you see both.

lessons.title: Say hello and who you are
lessons.summary: Greet someone, say your name and where you're from, and ask them the same: your first Portuguese conversation.
lessons.topic: {{ser}} “to be”: {{eu sou}}, {{você é}}; leaving out {{eu}}; {{de}} “from”

goal.t: Oi, meu nome é Sarah. Eu sou de Toronto.
goal.tr: Hi, my name is Sarah. I'm from Toronto.

dialog.t: Oi! Meu nome é Lucas.
dialog.tr: Hi! My name is Lucas.

dialog.t: Oi, Lucas! Meu nome é Sarah.
dialog.tr: Hi, Lucas! My name is Sarah.

dialog.t: Você é de onde?
dialog.tr: Where are you from?

dialog.t: Sou de Toronto, do Canadá. E você?

dialog.tr: I'm from São Paulo.

dialog.t: Muito prazer!

dialog.t: O prazer é meu.

blocks.p: Look at how Sarah says where she's from: {{eu sou}} “I am”. Lucas asks with {{você é}} “you are”. These are two forms of the same verb, {{ser}} “to be”.

blocks.means: a group of words that says something complete: I'm from Toronto.
a short word that stands for a person or a thing: I, you, he, she.
a word for an action or a state: speak, live, want, be.

blocks.p: **I and you.** {{eu}} is “I”. For “you”, Brazilians say {{você}} to everyone: a friend, a child, a stranger. Each one has its own form of the verb, so learn them together: {{eu sou}}, {{você é}}.
**Leaving out “I”.** {{sou}} can only mean “I am”, so Brazilians often drop {{eu}}: {{Sou de Toronto.}} Both are right.

**From.** {{de}} is “from”: {{de Toronto}}, {{de São Paulo}}. Most countries have a word for “the” in front of them, and {{de}} joins it: {{do Canadá}}, {{da Inglaterra}}, {{dos Estados Unidos}}. For now, learn your own as a chunk (a later lesson explains it), or say your nationality instead:
The second word ends in {{-o}} when a man says it and in {{-a}} when a woman does ({{canadense}} is the same for both): the next lesson explains why.

**Asking.** A question can have exactly the words of a statement: just raise your voice at the end. {{Você é de Toronto?}} “Are you from Toronto?” To ask where from, Brazilians usually put {{de onde}} “from where” at the end: {{Você é de onde?}} The textbook order, {{De onde você é?}}, is right too.

ex.tr: My name is Daniel.
I'm from Chicago.
Where are you from?

ex.t: Sou dos Estados Unidos. E você?
ex.tr: I'm from the United States. And you?
She's from Rio.
ex.note: Rio has “the” in front of it: {{do Rio}}

ex.tr: Nice to meet you!

blocks.tip: Hello and goodbye: {{Oi!}} is “Hi!” with anyone; {{Olá!}} is a little more formal. {{Bom dia}} (morning), {{Boa tarde}} (afternoon), {{Boa noite}} (evening, and goodnight). {{Tchau!}} is “Bye!”.

mistakes.why: With {{eu}}, the verb is {{sou}}. {{É}} goes with {{você}}, {{ele}} and {{ela}}.
Most cities have no “the” in Portuguese, so plain {{de}}: {{de Toronto}}, {{de Londres}}. {{Do}} is for places that take “the”, like {{do Canadá}} or {{do Rio}}.

lessons.title: Say how you are
lessons.summary: Answer “How are you?” and say how you feel today: tired, fine, happy, busy.
lessons.topic: {{estar}} “to be” (how you are now): {{estou}}, {{está}}; adjectives ending in {{-o}} or {{-a}}; {{ser}} or {{estar}}

goal.t: Estou muito bem, obrigado. E você?
goal.tr: I'm very well, thanks. And you?
goal.note: said by a man; a woman says {{obrigada}}

dialog.t: Oi, Pedro! Tudo bem?
dialog.tr: Hi, Pedro! How's it going?

dialog.t: Tudo bem, e você?
dialog.tr: Fine, and you?

dialog.t: Tudo ótimo! Mas estou um pouco cansada.
dialog.tr: Great! But I'm a little tired.

dialog.t: Eu também. Estou muito cansado hoje.
dialog.tr: Me too. I'm really tired today.

dialog.t: Vamos tomar um café?
dialog.tr: Shall we get a coffee?

dialog.t: Boa ideia!
dialog.tr: Good idea!

blocks.p: **How are you?** Brazilians greet each other with {{Tudo bem?}}, literally “All well?”, and the usual answer is the same words: {{Tudo bem!}} Or {{Tudo ótimo!}} “All great!”, {{Tudo certo!}} “All good!”.
**A second “to be”.** To say how you are right now, Portuguese uses another verb for “to be”: {{estar}}. {{Estou cansado}} “I'm tired”, {{Você está bem?}} “Are you OK?”.

Think of it like this: {{ser}} says what someone **is** (a name, where they're from, a job); {{estar}} says how someone **is at the moment** (tired, fine, busy, sick). {{Sou de Toronto}} won't change tomorrow; {{Estou cansado}} will pass. The two verbs come back many times in this course, each time for a new job.

blocks.means: a word that describes a person or a thing: tired, happy, big, new.

blocks.p: **Endings for men and women.** Most adjectives end in {{-o}} for a man and {{-a}} for a woman: Pedro is {{cansado}}, Carla is {{cansada}}. Those that end in {{-e}} or in a consonant usually stay the same: {{feliz}} “happy”, {{doente}} “sick”. Even “thank you” changes: a man says {{obrigado}}, a woman {{obrigada}} (it means “obliged”, so it describes the person speaking).

ex.tr: I'm fine, thanks.
I'm really tired today.
Are you busy?
She's sick.
I'm happy!
ex.note: the same for a man or a woman

ex.tr: So-so.

blocks.tip: In speech, {{está}} is often just {{tá}} and {{estou}} is {{tô}}: {{Tá bom!}} “OK!”, {{Tô cansado}} “I'm tired”. You'll hear them all day; write the full forms.

mistakes.why: Being tired is how you are right now: {{estar}}, not {{ser}}.
A woman says {{obrigada}}, with {{-a}}: the word describes the person speaking, not the one being thanked.

lessons.title: Answer yes and no like a Brazilian
lessons.summary: Say what you do and don't do, and answer questions the Brazilian way: with the verb, not just “yes”.
lessons.topic: {{não}} before the verb; answering with the verb ({{Fala? Falo.}}); {{falo}} “I speak”, {{fala}} “you speak”

goal.t: Entendo um pouco, mas não falo muito bem.
goal.tr: I understand a little, but I don't speak very well.

dialog.t: Você fala português?
dialog.tr: Do you speak Portuguese?

dialog.tr: I speak a little.

dialog.tr: Are you American?

dialog.tr: Do you live here?

dialog.t: Não, não moro. Estou de férias.
dialog.tr: No, I don't. I'm on vacation.

blocks.p: **Saying “not”.** Put {{não}} just before the verb: {{Falo inglês}} “I speak English”, {{Não falo inglês}} “I don't speak English”. Portuguese has no helper like “don't” or “doesn't”: {{não}} does the whole job.

blocks.means: who or what does the action of the verb: **I** speak, **Ana** lives here, **the bus** is late.

blocks.p: **The ending tells you who.** A Portuguese verb changes its ending for each subject. {{falo}} is “I speak”, {{fala}} is “you speak” (and also “he speaks”, “she speaks”). Here are a few everyday verbs in these two forms:
Because {{falo}} can only mean “I speak”, {{eu}} is usually left out. With {{fala}}, say {{você}}, {{ele}} or {{ela}} when it isn't clear who you mean.

**Saying yes.** {{Sim}} means “yes”, but Brazilians rarely answer with {{sim}} alone. They answer with the question's own verb, the way English says “I do” or “I am”: {{Você fala inglês? — Falo.}} Add {{sim}} after it to sound warm: {{Falo, sim.}}

**Saying no.** Say {{não}}, then {{não}} and the verb: {{Não, não falo.}} The first {{não}} is “no”, the second is “not”. In relaxed speech many Brazilians put one more at the very end: {{Não falo, não.}}

ex.tr: I don't understand.
Do you live here? — Yes, I do.
He doesn't work today.
I don't know.
Are you tired? — Yes, I am.
I don't know.
ex.note: the extra {{não}} at the end is relaxed, everyday speech

blocks.tip: Two lifesavers: {{Não entendo}} “I don't understand” and {{Pode repetir, por favor?}} “Could you say that again, please?”.

mistakes.tr: Do you speak English? — Yes, I do.
mistakes.why: Portuguese has no helper “do”: answer with the question's own verb, in the “I” form.

lessons.summary: Ask for food and drinks politely, and say what you want to do: “I'd like a coffee, please.”
lessons.topic: {{quero}} and the polite {{queria}}; {{um}} / {{uma}} “a”; masculine and feminine nouns

goal.t: Eu queria um café e um pão de queijo, por favor.

blocks.p: **Asking for things.** {{Quero}} is “I want”. {{Queria}} is softer, like “I'd like”: it's really “I wanted”, and it's what Brazilians say at a counter. Then say what you want: {{Queria um café.}}

blocks.means: a word for a person, a place or a thing: coffee, friend, city, water.
whether a noun is masculine or feminine. In Portuguese every noun has one, even a coffee or a table.
a little word in front of a noun: a, an, the.

blocks.p: **“A” has two forms.** Before a masculine noun it's {{um}}, before a feminine one {{uma}}: {{um café}}, {{uma água}}. Nouns that end in {{-o}} are usually masculine and those that end in {{-a}} usually feminine; for the others, learn each noun with its {{um}} or {{uma}}.

blocks.p: **Wanting to do something.** Put a second verb straight after {{quero}} or {{queria}}, in its basic form (the one that ends in {{-r}}): {{Quero pagar}} “I want to pay”, {{Queria ver o cardápio}} “I'd like to see the menu”. Portuguese needs no word for “to” here.

lessons.title: Point at things and name them
lessons.summary: Ask “What's that?”, name things, and say “the”, “this” and “that” in Portuguese.
lessons.topic: {{o, a, os, as}} “the”; the plural {{-s}}; {{esse}}, {{essa}}, {{aquele}}, {{isso}}

goal.t: O que é isso? É uma fruta?
goal.tr: What's that? Is it a fruit?

dialog.t: Com licença, o que é isso?
dialog.tr: Excuse me, what's that?

dialog.t: É um caju.
dialog.tr: It's a cashew fruit.

dialog.t: E essas frutas?

dialog.t: São mangas. Estão ótimas hoje!
dialog.tr: They're mangoes. They're great today!

dialog.t: Queria as mangas, por favor.
dialog.tr: I'd like the mangoes, please.

blocks.p: **What's that?** {{O que é isso?}} works for anything you point at. The answer starts with {{É}} “it is”: Portuguese has no word for “it” here, the verb says it on its own. For more than one thing, {{São}} “they are”: {{São mangas.}}

blocks.means: the form of a word for more than one: one house, two houses.

blocks.p: **“The” has four forms.** It changes for masculine and feminine, and for one or more than one:
Most plurals just add {{-s}}, and “the” adds it too: {{a manga}}, {{as mangas}}. (Words with other endings change in other ways; a later lesson shows the main ones.)

**This and that.** In everyday Brazilian speech, {{esse}} (masculine) and {{essa}} (feminine) mean “this” or “that” for something near you or the person you're talking to. {{aquele}}, {{aquela}} is “that one over there”. For a thing you don't name, use {{isso}} “this, that”, which never changes.

ex.tr: What's that?
It's a pen.
This book is good.
That's the station over there.
The books are expensive.
That's really expensive!

blocks.tip: You'll also see {{este}} and {{esta}} for “this” on signs and in writing ({{Este produto…}}). In conversation most Brazilians use {{esse}} and {{essa}} for both “this” and “that”.

mistakes.why: For a thing you don't name, use {{isso}}. {{Esse}} goes with a noun: {{esse livro}}.
{{Casa}} is feminine, so “the” is {{as}}.

lessons.title: Ask for information
lessons.summary: Ask who, what, where, when, how and why, and get to know someone.
lessons.topic: Question words: {{o que, onde, quem, quando, como, qual, quanto, por que}}; at the start or at the end

goal.t: Onde você mora e o que você faz?
goal.tr: Where do you live and what do you do?

dialog.t: Qual é o seu nome?
dialog.tr: What's your name?

dialog.t: Meu nome é Kate. E o seu?
dialog.tr: My name is Kate. And yours?

dialog.t: Rafael. Onde você mora?
dialog.tr: Rafael. Where do you live?

dialog.t: Moro em Boston. E você mora onde?
dialog.tr: I live in Boston. And where do you live?

dialog.t: Aqui em Belo Horizonte. O que você faz?
dialog.tr: Here in Belo Horizonte. What do you do?

dialog.t: Sou enfermeira. E você?
dialog.tr: I'm a nurse. And you?

blocks.means: a word that asks for information: what, where, who, when, how, why.

blocks.p: **The question word goes first, and nothing else changes.** Unlike English, Portuguese adds no “do” and swaps no words: {{Você mora em Boston}} “You live in Boston” → {{Onde você mora?}} “Where do you live?”.

table: {{O que você faz?}} What do you do?
{{Onde você mora?}} Where do you live?
{{Quando você chega?}} When do you arrive?
{{Qual é o seu nome?}} What's your name?
{{Por que você está aqui?}} Why are you here?

blocks.p: **Or at the end.** In conversation Brazilians often leave the question word at the end, where the answer would go: {{Você mora onde?}}, {{Você faz o quê?}} It sounds relaxed, or surprised. At the very end, {{que}} takes an accent: {{o quê}}. Both orders are right.

**{{Qual}} or {{o que}}?** For “what is…?” when you want a name, a number or one of several, Brazilians say {{qual}}: {{Qual é o seu nome?}}, {{Qual é o seu telefone?}} {{O que é…?}} asks what something is: {{O que é caju?}} “What's a caju?”.

ex.tr: Who is she?
When is the party?
What's your name?
What's your phone number?
Why are you sad?

ex.t: Como se diz isso em português?
ex.tr: How do you say this in Portuguese?
ex.note: a question you'll use every day

blocks.tip: Kate answers {{Sou enfermeira}} “I'm a nurse”: with jobs, Portuguese uses no {{um}} or {{uma}}. {{Sou professor}}, {{Sou médica}}.

mistakes.wrong: O que é o seu nome?
mistakes.why: Before {{é}}, “what” is {{qual}} when you're asking for a name, a number or a choice. {{O que é…?}} asks what something is.
“Why” in a question is two words, {{por que}}. Written as one, {{porque}} means “because” (a later lesson).

lessons.title: Say where things and places are
lessons.summary: Ask where a place is, say where you are, and use “in”, “near” and “next to”.
lessons.topic: {{ficar}} for places, {{estar}} for things and people; {{em}} + “the” = {{no}}, {{na}}; {{perto de}}, {{longe de}}

goal.t: Com licença, onde fica o banheiro?
goal.tr: Excuse me, where's the bathroom?

dialog.t: Com licença, onde fica a estação de metrô?
dialog.tr: Excuse me, where's the subway station?

dialog.t: Fica perto daqui, do lado do banco.
dialog.tr: It's near here, next to the bank.

dialog.t: Fica longe?
dialog.tr: Is it far?

dialog.t: Não, fica a cinco minutos a pé.
dialog.tr: No, it's five minutes' walk.

dialog.t: Muito obrigado!
dialog.tr: Thanks a lot!

dialog.t: De nada!
dialog.tr: You're welcome!

blocks.p: **Where is it?** For places that don't move (a station, a bank, a city), Brazilians ask with {{ficar}}: {{Onde fica o banheiro?}} “Where's the bathroom?”. {{Fica}} literally means “stays”, and the answer uses it too: {{Fica ali.}} “It's over there.” You'll also hear {{Onde é…?}}, with the same meaning.

For people and things that move (your phone, the keys, a friend), use {{estar}}, the verb for how and where something is right now: {{Onde está o meu celular?}} “Where's my phone?”, {{Estou no ônibus}} “I'm on the bus”.

blocks.means: a little word that links a noun to the rest of the sentence, often to say where or when: in, on, at, near, from.
two words said and written as one, like “don't” for “do not”.

blocks.p: **In, on, at: all {{em}}.** One Portuguese preposition, {{em}}, covers “in”, “on” and “at”. And it joins “the” into one word:

Cities have no “the”, so plain {{em}}: {{em São Paulo}}, {{em Londres}}. And {{de}} joins “the” the same way: {{do}}, {{da}}, {{dos}}, {{das}}. That's the {{do Canadá}} of the first lesson: “from the Canada”.
**Near, far, next to.** These end in {{de}}, which then joins “the” as usual:

ex.t: O banheiro fica no segundo andar.
ex.tr: The bathroom is on the second floor.
My phone is on the table.

ex.t: A farmácia fica perto do hotel.
ex.tr: The pharmacy is near the hotel.

ex.t: Moro em Curitiba, perto do centro.
ex.tr: I live in Curitiba, near downtown.

ex.t: Onde você está? — Estou no ônibus.
ex.tr: Where are you? — I'm on the bus.
Is it far from here?

blocks.tip: Brazilians often put {{o}} or {{a}} before people's names, like a friendly “the”: {{O Pedro está em casa}}, {{a Ana}}. It's normal in most of Brazil: do it or leave it out.

mistakes.wrong: O livro está em a mesa.
mistakes.tr: The book is on the table.
mistakes.why: {{Em}} and {{a}} always join: {{na}}.
Cities have no “the”, so plain {{em}}.

lessons.title: Ask what there is nearby
lessons.summary: Ask if there's a pharmacy, an ATM or wi-fi, and say what there is and isn't.
lessons.topic: {{tem}} “there is, there are” (in writing {{há}}); {{tem}} or {{está}}

goal.t: Tem uma farmácia aqui perto?
goal.tr: Is there a pharmacy near here?

dialog.t: Boa noite! Tem um restaurante aqui perto?

blocks.p: **There is, there are: {{tem}}.** In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, “there is” and “there are” are both just {{tem}} (literally “it has”): {{Tem um banco aqui.}} “There's a bank here.” {{Tem muitas pessoas.}} “There are a lot of people.” It never changes, for one thing or for many.

To ask, raise your voice: {{Tem…?}} And answer with the verb, the Brazilian way: {{Tem, sim.}} / {{Não tem.}} In a question, Brazilians often drop {{um/uma}}: {{Tem farmácia aqui perto?}} “Is there a pharmacy near here?”, {{Tem água?}} “Is there any water?”.

**In writing: {{há}}.** Books, signs and the news use {{há}} for the same thing: {{Há um banco aqui.}} You'll read it everywhere and hear it in formal moments; in conversation, {{tem}} is what people say.

**{{tem}} or {{está}}?** {{Tem}} says that something exists somewhere; {{estar}} and {{ficar}} say where one particular thing is. {{Tem um banco na praça}} “There's a bank in the square”; {{O banco fica na praça}} “The bank is in the square”.

ex.t: Tem um caixa eletrônico aqui perto?
ex.tr: Is there an ATM near here?

ex.tr: There are a lot of people on the beach today.
There's no room.
Is there wi-fi at the hotel?

ex.note: on a sign, or in formal speech

ex.tr: What is there to eat?

blocks.tip: {{Tem}} also means “has”: {{Ela tem um carro}} “She has a car” (three lessons from now). So {{Tem café?}} is “Is there coffee?” or “Do you have coffee?”: in a café, it's the same question!

lessons.topic: Numbers ({{um/uma}}, {{dois/duas}}); plurals ({{reais}}, {{pães}}, {{hotéis}}); {{Quanto custa?}} and {{Quanto custam?}}

goal.t: Quanto custam duas águas e um café?

blocks.p: **One and two have genders.** “One” is {{um}} or {{uma}}, the same words as “a”, and “two” is {{dois}} or {{duas}}: {{dois cafés}}, {{duas águas}}. From three on, numbers stay the same for every noun.

Then the tens: {{trinta}} 30, {{quarenta}} 40, {{cinquenta}} 50, {{sessenta}} 60, {{setenta}} 70, {{oitenta}} 80, {{noventa}} 90, {{cem}} 100. In between, join with {{e}} “and”: {{vinte e cinco}} 25, {{trinta e duas}} 32 (with a feminine noun), {{cento e dez}} 110.
**Plurals.** Most words add {{-s}}, as you know. A few common endings change:
Words in {{-ão}} have three plurals: {{-ões}} is the most common ({{limões}}), but {{pães}}, {{alemães}} and {{mãos}} have their own, so learn them as you meet them.

**Prices.** {{Quanto custa?}} “How much is it?” for one thing, {{Quanto custam?}} for more than one. To ask for the total, {{Quanto é?}} “How much is it?”. Brazil's money is the {{real}}, plural {{reais}}; cents are {{centavos}}. Brazilians write a comma where English has a point: R$ 4,50 is {{quatro e cinquenta}}.

ex.tr: How much is this hat?
How much are the T-shirts?
It's twenty-five reais.

lessons.title: Describe people and things
lessons.summary: Say what people, places and things are like: big, nice, old, beautiful.
lessons.topic: Adjectives after the noun, matching it; {{ser}} + adjective; {{é bonito}} or {{está bonito}}; {{somos}}, {{são}}

goal.t: O Rio é uma cidade linda, mas é muito cara.
goal.tr: Rio is a beautiful city, but it's really expensive.

dialog.t: E o apartamento novo?
dialog.tr: So how's the new apartment?

dialog.tr: It's quiet and there are lots of trees.

blocks.p: **After the noun.** Adjectives usually come after the noun in Portuguese: {{uma cidade bonita}} “a pretty city”, {{um carro novo}} “a new car”.
**They match the noun.** An adjective takes the gender and the number of its noun, so many have four forms:

Adjectives ending in {{-e}} or in a consonant have one form for both genders, and add {{-s}} or {{-es}} for the plural: {{um homem inteligente}}, {{mulheres inteligentes}}; {{um dia feliz}}, {{dias felizes}}.

**What something is like: {{ser}}.** To describe a person or a thing, use {{ser}}: {{O apartamento é pequeno.}} {{Os vizinhos são simpáticos.}} Here are both “to be” verbs in full. {{vocês}} is “you” to more than one person.

**{{é bonito}} or {{está bonito}}?** With {{estar}}, an adjective says how something is now, or how it looks today. {{A sopa é boa}}: it's a good soup. {{A sopa está boa}}: it tastes good right now. {{Você é bonita}} “You're beautiful”; {{Você está bonita!}} “You look nice today!”.

ex.t: Ela é alta e muito inteligente.
ex.tr: She's tall and really smart.

ex.t: Meu carro é velho, mas é bom.
ex.tr: My car is old, but it's good.
The beaches are beautiful.
The coffee is cold.
Are you Brazilian?
What a beautiful day!

blocks.tip: A few short adjectives often go before the noun: {{um bom restaurante}}, {{uma boa ideia}}. {{Grande}} before the noun means “great”, after it “big”: {{um grande amigo}} “a great friend”, {{uma casa grande}} “a big house”.

lessons.topic: {{ter}} “to have” ({{tenho, tem, temos, têm}}); age with {{ter}}; {{meu/minha}}, {{seu/sua}}, {{nosso/nossa}}

goal.t: Tenho dois irmãos e uma irmã.

dialog.t: Você tem irmãos?

dialog.t: Tenho, sim. Tenho uma irmã. E você?

blocks.p: **To have: {{ter}}.** {{Tenho}} is “I have”, {{tem}} “you have, he/she has”: the same {{tem}} as “there is”.
{{Têm}} sounds just like {{tem}}: the little hat only shows, in writing, that it's plural.
**Age: you “have” years.** Portuguese says how old you are with {{ter}}: {{Tenho trinta anos}}, literally “I have thirty years”. To ask: {{Quantos anos você tem?}} “How old are you?”.

blocks.means: a word that says whose something is: my, your, his, our.

blocks.p: **My, your, our.** {{meu}} and {{minha}} are “my”, {{seu}} and {{sua}} “your” (to {{você}}), {{nosso}} and {{nossa}} “our”. They match the thing you have, not the person who has it: a man says {{minha casa}}, because {{casa}} is feminine, and a woman says {{meu carro}}.
Brazilians often put “the” before them, {{a minha casa}}, {{o meu carro}}: with it or without it is right.

**Family.** {{pai}} father, {{mãe}} mother, {{irmão}} brother, {{irmã}} sister, {{filho}} son, {{filha}} daughter, {{marido}} husband, {{esposa}} wife, {{namorado}}, {{namorada}} boyfriend, girlfriend. A masculine plural covers a mixed group: {{irmãos}} is “brothers” or “brothers and sisters”, {{filhos}} “sons” or “children”, {{pais}} “parents”.

lessons.title: Say where you're going and how
lessons.summary: Say where you're going, ask others, and say how you'll get there: by bus, by car, on foot.
lessons.topic: {{ir}} “to go” ({{vou, vai, vamos, vão}}); {{a}} and {{para}} ({{pra}}) + “the”: {{ao, à, pro, pra}}; {{de ônibus}}, {{a pé}}

goal.t: Hoje eu vou pra praia. Vamos?
goal.tr: I'm going to the beach today. Shall we go?

blocks.p: **To go: {{ir}}.** It's irregular, and you'll use it all day long:
**“To” a place: {{a}} or {{para}}.** After {{ir}}, “to” is {{a}} (a little careful) or {{para}} (everyday), which in speech shrinks to {{pra}}: {{Vou pra casa}} “I'm going home”. Both join “the”:
The accent on {{à}} shows that two {{a}}'s have become one: “to” + “the”. Cities and “home” have no “the”: {{Vou a São Paulo}}, {{Vou pra casa}}.
**Where to?** {{Aonde você vai?}} “Where are you going?” ({{a}} + {{onde}}). In speech you'll also hear {{Onde você vai?}} and {{Você vai pra onde?}}
**How: {{de}}.** {{de ônibus}} by bus, {{de carro}} by car, {{de metrô}} by subway, {{de táxi}}, {{de avião}} by plane, {{de bicicleta}} by bike. But on foot is {{a pé}}.

We're going to the beach tomorrow.

lessons.summary: Say where you live and work and what you do, for yourself and for others: the present tense of regular verbs.
lessons.topic: The present: regular {{-ar}}, {{-er}}, {{-ir}} verbs; {{nós}} and {{a gente}} “we”; {{num}}, {{numa}}

goal.t: Eu trabalho num hospital e moro perto do centro.
goal.tr: I work in a hospital and live near downtown.

dialog.t: Você trabalha com quê?
dialog.tr: What do you do for work?

dialog.t: Sou engenheiro. Trabalho numa empresa de energia.

dialog.t: E você mora aqui no bairro?

dialog.t: E vocês falam português em casa?

dialog.t: Não, a gente fala inglês. Mas eu estudo português todo dia!

blocks.means: the basic form of a verb, the one in the dictionary: to speak, to eat. In Portuguese it ends in {{-r}}: {{falar}}, {{comer}}, {{abrir}}.

blocks.p: **Three families of verbs.** Every Portuguese infinitive ends in {{-ar}}, {{-er}} or {{-ir}}. To use a verb, take off those two letters and add the ending for who does it:

**Four forms are enough.** In Brazil, {{você}} “you”, {{ele}} “he”, {{ela}} “she” and {{a gente}} “we” share one form, and {{vocês}} “you all”, {{eles}} and {{elas}} “they” share another. (In some regions you'll hear {{tu}} for “you”, often with the same verb form as {{você}}.)

**Two ways to say “we”.** {{nós}} takes {{-mos}}: {{nós falamos}}. But in conversation Brazilians usually say {{a gente}} (literally “the people”), with the same form as {{ele}}: {{a gente fala}}. Both mean “we speak”; {{a gente}} sounds relaxed, {{nós}} a little more careful.
**{{num}}, {{numa}}.** {{Em}} also joins {{um}} and {{uma}}: {{num banco}} “in a bank”, {{numa empresa}} “at a company”.

She works from home.

ex.tr: We eat a lot of rice and beans.
We open at nine.

lessons.title: Say what you like
lessons.summary: Say what you like, love and hate, ask others, and agree: “Me too!”, “Me neither!”.
lessons.topic: {{gostar de}} (with {{do}}, {{da}}); {{adorar}}, {{odiar}}; {{eu também}}, {{eu também não}}

goal.t: Eu adoro café, mas não gosto de chá.
goal.tr: I love coffee, but I don't like tea.

dialog.t: Você gosta de comida brasileira?
dialog.tr: Do you like Brazilian food?

dialog.t: Gosto muito! Adoro feijoada.
dialog.tr: I really do! I love feijoada.

dialog.t: E de música? Você gosta de samba?

dialog.t: Gosto, mas gosto mais de bossa nova.
dialog.tr: I do, but I like bossa nova more.

dialog.t: Eu também! E você gosta de dançar?

dialog.t: Não, não gosto. Danço muito mal!
dialog.tr: No, I don't. I dance really badly!

blocks.p: **{{gostar de}}.** “To like” is {{gostar}}, and it always takes {{de}} before what you like: {{Gosto de café.}} “I like coffee.” That {{de}} joins “the” as usual: {{Gosto do Brasil}}, {{Gosto da praia}}.
After {{de}}, a verb stays in its infinitive: {{Gosto de ler}} “I like reading”.
**Love it, hate it.** {{adorar}} “love” and {{odiar}} “hate” take no {{de}}: {{Adoro praia}}, {{Odeio acordar cedo}}. Brazilians say {{adoro}} about things all the time.

**How much.** {{muito}} “a lot”, {{mais}} “more” and {{um pouco}} “a little” come right after {{gosto}}: {{Gosto muito de você}} “I really like you”. And to agree: {{Eu também}} “Me too”, {{Eu também não}} “Me neither” (literally “I also not”).
**What do you like?** {{Do que você gosta?}}, or in relaxed speech {{Você gosta de quê?}}, with {{quê}} at the end, as in lesson 6.

ex.tr: I really like traveling.

ex.t: Ela não gosta de acordar cedo.
ex.tr: She doesn't like getting up early.
Do you like the city?
I love this restaurant!

ex.t: Não gosto de futebol. — Eu também não.
ex.tr: I don't like soccer. — Me neither.

ex.t: O que você gosta de fazer no fim de semana?
ex.tr: What do you like to do on the weekend?

blocks.tip: {{Gosto de você}} is “I like you”; {{Eu te amo}} is “I love you” ({{te}} is “you”: lesson 24 shows how it works).

mistakes.why: {{Gostar}} always takes {{de}} before what you like.
{{De}} and {{o}} join: {{do}}.

lessons.summary: Ask and tell the time, say when things happen, and talk about the days of the week.
lessons.topic: {{Que horas são?}}; {{São duas.}} / {{É uma.}}; {{às três}}; {{de manhã}}; {{no sábado}}, {{na segunda}}, {{toda sexta}}

goal.t: A aula começa às oito, de segunda a sexta.

blocks.p: **What time is it?** {{Que horas são?}} The answer starts with {{são}} “they are” (the hours are plural), but with {{é}} for one o'clock, noon and midnight. Hours are feminine ({{a hora}}), so {{uma}}, {{duas}}:
{{Meia}} is “half” (of an hour). {{Quinze pras quatro}} is “fifteen to four”.

**At what time?** Ask {{Que horas…?}} or {{A que horas…?}}; answer with {{às}} and the hour: {{às duas}}, {{às oito e meia}}. That's the {{à}} of lesson 12, “at the”. But {{à uma}} (one), {{ao meio-dia}}, {{à meia-noite}}. From… to…: {{das nove às seis}}.
**Parts of the day.** {{de manhã}} in the morning, {{à tarde}} in the afternoon, {{à noite}} at night. With an hour: {{às oito da manhã}}, {{às três da tarde}}, {{às dez da noite}}.

**Days.** Brazilians number the weekdays: {{segunda-feira}} Monday (“second day”), {{terça}} Tuesday, {{quarta}} Wednesday, {{quinta}} Thursday, {{sexta}} Friday; then {{sábado}} and {{domingo}}. The {{-feira}} is usually dropped. Monday to Friday are feminine, Saturday and Sunday masculine:

ex.tr: What time is it? — It's ten twenty.

ex.t: O ônibus sai às sete e meia.

The store opens at noon.

blocks.tip: Timetables, tickets and TV use the 24-hour clock: {{às 19h}} is read {{às dezenove horas}}. In conversation people say {{às sete da noite}}.

“At” a time is {{às}}, “at the (hours)”.

blocks.p: **Irregular verbs.** The most-used verbs don't quite follow lesson 13's pattern, especially in the “I” form. Here are eight you need to talk about your week:
Most of the surprise is in the “I” form; the others stay close to the regular pattern. {{Vêm}} “they come” has a hat; {{vem}} “comes” doesn't.

**{{fazer}}: do and make.** One verb for both: {{fazer o jantar}} “make dinner”, {{fazer exercício}} “exercise”, {{fazer compras}} “go shopping”. And the question about anyone's job or plans: {{O que você faz?}}

**{{ir}} or {{vir}}?** {{Vir}} “come” is only toward the place where the speaker is. Chris is going to Marina's house, so he says {{Posso ir?}}, not {{Posso vir?}} And “I'm coming!” to someone calling you is {{Já vou!}}
**{{ver}}: see and watch.** {{ver TV}}, {{ver um filme}}: “watch TV, watch a movie”. ({{Assistir}} also means “watch”: {{assistir a um filme}}.)

ex.tr: We watch a movie every Friday.
I come here every day.
I always bring the wine.
I don't know what to say.

ex.tr: I work out at the gym three times a week.

blocks.tip: {{Sabe?}} at the end of a sentence is “you know?”: {{Eu adoro bolo, sabe?}} You'll hear it constantly.

lessons.title: Describe your morning routine
lessons.summary: Say when you wake up, get up and get ready, and introduce yourself the everyday way: “Me chamo…”.
lessons.topic: Reflexive verbs: {{me levanto}}, {{se chama}}, {{nos vemos}}; the pronoun before the verb, as Brazilians say it

goal.t: Eu acordo às seis, tomo banho e me visto rápido.
goal.tr: I wake up at six, shower and get dressed quickly.

dialog.t: Você acorda cedo?
dialog.tr: Do you wake up early?

dialog.t: Acordo às seis, mas só me levanto às seis e meia.

dialog.t: E você toma café da manhã?

dialog.t: Tomo, sim. Depois eu me arrumo e saio às sete e meia.

dialog.t: Nossa, eu me atraso todo dia!

blocks.means: a verb whose action goes back to the subject: you do it to yourself. In English: I hurt myself, enjoy yourself.

blocks.p: **Doing it to yourself.** Many everyday actions are reflexive in Portuguese: you “raise yourself” ({{levantar-se}}, get up), “dress yourself” ({{vestir-se}}), “call yourself” ({{chamar-se}}). The verb takes a small pronoun that matches the subject:

**Before the verb, as Brazilians say it.** In Brazil the pronoun goes before the verb: {{Eu me levanto às sete.}} Dictionaries write {{levantar-se}}, with the pronoun after, and so does careful writing; but in Brazilian speech even a sentence can start with it: {{Me chamo Dan.}} “My name is Dan.”

Some reflexive routine verbs: {{me levanto}} I get up, {{me visto}} I get dressed, {{me arrumo}} I get ready, {{me deito}} I lie down, {{me atraso}} I'm late, {{me sinto}} I feel. Others aren't reflexive: {{acordar}} wake up, {{tomar banho}} shower, {{tomar café}} have breakfast or coffee, {{escovar os dentes}} brush your teeth, {{sair}} leave.
**Each other.** With a plural subject, {{se}} and {{nos}} can mean “each other”: {{A gente se vê amanhã!}} “See you tomorrow!” (literally “We see each other tomorrow”).

ex.t: Me chamo Daniel. E você, como se chama?
ex.tr: My name is Daniel. And you, what's your name?
She gets up at five.

ex.t: Eu me visto e tomo café.
ex.tr: I get dressed and have breakfast.
We see each other every day.
Do you feel OK?

blocks.tip: {{Tomar}} is a busy verb: {{tomar banho}} take a shower, {{tomar café}} have coffee or breakfast, {{tomar um remédio}} take a medicine, {{tomar uma cerveja}} have a beer, {{tomar sol}} sunbathe.

mistakes.why: With {{eu}}, the pronoun is {{me}}; {{se}} goes with {{você}}, {{ele}}, {{ela}}, {{a gente}} and {{eles}}.
The pronoun matches the subject: {{ele se chama}}. ({{Ele me chama}} means “he calls me”.)

lessons.title: Say what's happening right now
lessons.summary: Say what you're doing at the moment, ask others, and talk about the weather: “It's raining.”
lessons.topic: {{estar}} + the {{-ndo}} form ({{estou falando}}); the present for habits, {{estar}} + {{-ndo}} for now

goal.t: O que você está fazendo? — Estou vendo um filme.
goal.tr: What are you doing? — I'm watching a movie.

dialog.t: Alô? Oi, Kelly! O que você está fazendo?
dialog.tr: Hello? Hi, Kelly! What are you doing?

dialog.t: Estou estudando português. E você?
dialog.tr: I'm studying Portuguese. And you?

dialog.t: Estou saindo do trabalho. Vamos jantar?

dialog.t: Vamos! Mas está chovendo muito aqui.
dialog.tr: Sure! But it's raining a lot here.

dialog.t: Sem problema, eu vou de carro.

blocks.means: the “-ing” form of a verb: speaking, eating, going. In Portuguese it ends in {{-ndo}}.

blocks.p: **Right now: {{estar}} + {{-ndo}}.** For something happening at this moment, Brazilians use {{estar}} and the verb's {{-ndo}} form, just like English “am …-ing”: {{Estou trabalhando.}} “I'm working.”
To make the {{-ndo}} form, take the {{-r}} off the infinitive and add {{-ndo}}. It works for every verb, even the irregular ones:

Only {{estar}} changes for the person: {{estou falando}}, {{você está falando}}, {{estamos falando}}, {{eles estão falando}}. A reflexive pronoun goes just before the {{-ndo}} form: {{Estou me arrumando}} “I'm getting ready”.

**Usually or now?** {{Trabalho num banco}}: that's my job, every day. {{Estou trabalhando}}: I'm doing it right now. Brazilians also use {{estar}} + {{-ndo}} for what's going on these days: {{Estou morando em Lisboa}} “I'm living in Lisbon (for now)”.
**The weather.** No “it”, as usual: {{Está chovendo}} “It's raining”, {{Está fazendo frio}} “It's cold”, {{Está fazendo calor}} “It's hot”.

ex.tr: I'm studying for a test.
She's sleeping.
What are you guys doing?
It's raining a lot.
I'm almost there!
ex.note: literally “I'm arriving”: what Brazilians text on their way

ex.tr: I'm living with some friends (for now).

blocks.tip: In Portugal you'd hear {{estou a falar}}; in Brazil it's always {{estou falando}}.

mistakes.why: The {{-ndo}} form needs {{estar}} before it, like “am” in English.
The ending comes from the infinitive: {{fazer}} → {{fazendo}}.

lessons.summary: Say what you're going to do tonight, tomorrow and next year, and ask about other people's plans.
lessons.topic: {{ir}} + infinitive ({{vou viajar}}); {{semana que vem}}, {{amanhã}}, {{hoje à noite}}; {{vou}} alone for “going to go”

goal.t: Amanhã eu vou visitar meus avós.

blocks.p: **{{ir}} + infinitive.** To talk about the future, Brazilians nearly always use {{ir}} and a second verb in its infinitive, exactly like English “going to”: {{Vou viajar}} “I'm going to travel”. You already know {{ir}}: {{vou, vai, vamos, vão}}.

table: Are you going to work tomorrow?

blocks.p: **“Not” goes before {{vou}}:** {{Não vou sair hoje.}} A reflexive pronoun goes before the second verb: {{Vou me arrumar.}}

**Going to go.** For “I'm going to go”, Brazilians usually just say {{vou}}: {{Amanhã vou à praia}} “Tomorrow I'm going to the beach”. You'll also hear {{vou ir}} in relaxed speech, but many people find it clumsy.

**When.** {{hoje à noite}} tonight, {{amanhã}} tomorrow, {{depois de amanhã}} the day after tomorrow, {{semana que vem}} next week, {{mês que vem}} next month, {{ano que vem}} next year, {{daqui a pouco}} in a little while, {{mais tarde}} later.

lessons.title: Say what you can and can't do
lessons.summary: Ask for permission and favors, say what you know how to do, and what you can't manage: four kinds of “can”.
lessons.topic: {{poder}} (allowed, favors), {{saber}} (know how), {{conseguir}} (manage), {{dá pra}} (it's possible)

goal.t: Você pode me ajudar? Não consigo abrir a porta.
goal.tr: Can you help me? I can't open the door.

dialog.t: Com licença, você pode me ajudar?
dialog.tr: Excuse me, can you help me?

dialog.t: Claro! Pois não?
dialog.tr: Of course! What can I do for you?

dialog.t: Não consigo abrir a porta do quarto.
dialog.tr: I can't open the door to my room.

dialog.t: Ah, o cartão às vezes não funciona. Posso ver?

dialog.t: Pode. Aqui está.
dialog.tr: Sure. Here it is.

dialog.t: Pronto, agora dá pra abrir.

blocks.p: English has one “can”. Portuguese has four common ways to say it, each with its own job:

table: be allowed; asking favors; be free to
{{Dá pra ir a pé?}} Can you walk there?

blocks.p: **{{poder}}** is irregular in the “I” form: {{posso}}, {{pode}}, {{podemos}}, {{podem}}. It asks and gives permission ({{Posso sentar aqui?}} — {{Pode!}}) and asks favors ({{Você pode fechar a janela?}}).
**{{saber}}** is for skills: {{Você sabe dirigir?}} “Can you drive?” With {{poder}}, that question would mean “Are you allowed to drive?”.
**{{conseguir}}** “manage” is for things that don't work right now: {{Não consigo ouvir}} “I can't hear”. Forms: {{consigo}}, {{consegue}}, {{conseguimos}}, {{conseguem}}.

**{{dá pra}}** (from {{dar para}}, literally “it gives for”) is how Brazilians say “it's possible”: {{Dá pra pagar com cartão?}} “Can I pay by card?” The answer: {{Dá!}} or {{Não dá.}} And {{Não vai dar}} is the classic, polite “I can't make it”.
All four take an infinitive straight after: {{posso ir}}, {{sei cozinhar}}, {{consigo ver}}, {{dá pra ver}}. A pronoun goes before that second verb: {{Você pode me ajudar?}}

ex.tr: Can I sit here? — Sure, of course.
Can you speak Spanish?

ex.t: Não consigo dormir com esse barulho.
ex.tr: I can't sleep with this noise.
Can I pay by card?

I can't make it today, sorry.

blocks.tip: {{Pode deixar!}} means “Leave it to me!”: a friendly way to say you'll take care of something.

mistakes.why: A skill you've learned is {{saber}}.
Trying and failing is {{conseguir}}. {{Não posso}} would mean you're not allowed to.

blocks.p: **Have to: {{ter que}}.** The everyday way to say you must do something: {{ter}} + {{que}} + infinitive. {{Tenho que ir}} “I have to go”. (In writing you'll also see {{ter de}}, with the same meaning.)
**Need: {{precisar}}.** Before a verb, nothing in between: {{Preciso ir}} “I need to go”. Before a noun, {{precisar de}}: {{Preciso de ajuda}} “I need help”.

**Should: {{dever}}.** {{Você deve descansar}} “You should rest”. Brazilians soften advice with {{devia}} (“ought to”): {{Você devia ir ao médico}}. And {{deve}} + {{estar}} is a guess: {{Você deve estar cansado}} “You must be tired”.
**Not having to.** {{Não tenho que}} or {{Não preciso}}: {{Não precisa trazer nada}} “You don't need to bring anything”.

ex.tr: I have to work on Saturday.
Do you need help?

ex.t: A gente tem que comprar pão.
ex.tr: We have to buy bread.
You don't need to bring anything!
You ought to sleep more.
She must be at home.

blocks.tip: {{Tem que}} also says how things must be done, for anyone: {{Tem que apertar o botão}} “You have to press the button”.

mistakes.why: “Have to” needs {{que}}: {{ter que}} + infinitive.
Before a noun, {{precisar}} takes {{de}}.

lessons.title: Invite someone and make suggestions
lessons.summary: Invite a friend, suggest a plan, and say yes or no politely, the Brazilian way.
lessons.topic: {{Vamos…?}}, {{Que tal…?}}, {{Você quer…?}}, {{A gente pode…}}; {{comigo}}; soft ways to say no

goal.t: Que tal um cinema hoje à noite?
goal.tr: How about a movie tonight?

dialog.t: E aí, vamos fazer alguma coisa no sábado?

dialog.t: Vamos! Que tal ir à praia?

blocks.p: **Let's: {{vamos}} + infinitive.** {{Vamos comer?}} “Shall we eat?”; {{Vamos!}} “Let's!” With a place, it's the {{ir}} you know: {{Vamos à praia?}}
**How about…?: {{Que tal…?}}** With a noun or a verb: {{Que tal um café?}} “How about a coffee?”, {{Que tal sair mais cedo?}} “How about leaving earlier?”.
**Do you want to…?: {{Você quer…?}}** {{Você quer jantar comigo?}} “Do you want to have dinner with me?” ({{comigo}} is “with me”, one word.)
**We could…: {{A gente pode…}}**, the {{poder}} of lesson 20: {{A gente pode ver um filme}} “We could watch a movie”.

table: Do you want to come along?

blocks.p: **Saying yes.** {{Vamos!}}, {{Boa!}} “Good idea!”, {{Claro!}}, {{Adoraria!}} “I'd love to!”, {{Combinado!}} or {{Fechado!}} “Deal!”.

**Saying no, politely.** Brazilians rarely give a flat {{não}}: they soften it and give a reason. {{Ah, hoje não vai dar}} “Oh, today won't work”, {{Que pena, tenho que trabalhar}} “What a pity, I have to work”, {{Fica pra próxima}} “Let's leave it for next time”.

How about Saturday?

lessons.title: Ask and tell people to do things
lessons.summary: Give directions, ask for things at the table, and read signs and instructions: the two kinds of commands.
lessons.topic: Commands: the spoken form ({{fala}}, {{vira}}, {{me passa}}) and the written, polite form ({{fale}}, {{vire}}, {{faça}}); {{não}} + command

goal.t: Me passa o sal, por favor?
goal.tr: Could you pass me the salt, please?

dialog.t: Com licença, como chego ao museu?
dialog.tr: Excuse me, how do I get to the museum?

dialog.t: É fácil. Segue reto até o semáforo e vira à direita.
dialog.tr: It's easy. Go straight to the traffic light and turn right.

dialog.t: Viro à direita no semáforo…

dialog.tr: Thank you so much!

dialog.t: De nada. Ah, e cuidado com o trânsito!

blocks.means: the form of a verb for telling or asking someone to do something: Come here! Turn left.

blocks.p: **In conversation: the {{você}} form.** When Brazilians tell a friend, or a stranger asking the way, to do something, they mostly use the same form as {{você fala}}, {{ele faz}}: {{Fala mais alto!}} “Speak up!”, {{Vira à direita}} “Turn right”, {{Olha!}} “Look!”. A pronoun comes first: {{Me liga!}} “Call me!”, {{Me passa o sal}} “Pass me the salt”.

**In writing and polite speech: a different ending.** Signs, instructions, ads and polite service talk use another form: {{-ar}} verbs end in {{-e}}, and {{-er}} and {{-ir}} verbs in {{-a}}. It's built on the “I” form of the present, so irregular verbs keep their surprise: {{faço}} → {{faça}}, {{venho}} → {{venha}}.

You'll see the second form on every sign: {{Empurre}} “Push”, {{Puxe}} “Pull”, {{Aperte o botão}} “Press the button”, {{Fale conosco}} “Contact us”. A shop assistant may say {{Espere um momento}} “One moment, please”. (This form has a name, the subjunctive; lesson 38 shows its other jobs.)
**Don't.** Put {{não}} in front. In relaxed speech: {{Não esquece!}} “Don't forget!”; in writing and polite speech: {{Não esqueça}}, {{Não fume}} “No smoking”.
**Softening.** A bare command can sound bossy. Add {{por favor}}, or make it a question with a rising voice: {{Me passa o sal?}}, {{Você pode fechar a porta?}}

Come here!
Send me a message.

Don't say that!

The written command comes from the “I” form: {{faço}} → {{faça}}.

lessons.title: Talk about people and things without repeating them
lessons.summary: Say “me”, “you”, “him”, “it” and “us” as Brazilians do in conversation, and recognise the forms of careful writing.
lessons.topic: Object pronouns {{me}}, {{te}}, {{nos}}, {{lhe}} before the verb; “him, her, it” in speech ({{ele}}, {{ela}}, or nothing) and in writing ({{o}}, {{a}}); {{comigo}}, {{pra mim}}

goal.t: Eu te ligo amanhã. Você me espera?
goal.tr: I'll call you tomorrow. Will you wait for me?

dialog.t: Você conhece o Rafa?
dialog.tr: Do you know Rafa?

dialog.t: Conheço! Ele sempre me ajuda com o português.
dialog.tr: I do! He always helps me with my Portuguese.

dialog.t: Ele vai dar uma festa no sábado. Quer o telefone dele?

dialog.t: Passo. E eu te encontro lá!

blocks.means: the person or thing that receives the action of the verb: I see **you**, she calls **me**, we buy **bread**.

blocks.p: **Me, you, us.** These short pronouns go **before** the verb in Brazilian Portuguese:

table: {{Posso lhe perguntar uma coisa?}} May I ask you something?

blocks.p: Yes, {{te}} goes with {{você}}: Brazilians mix the two all the time, and {{Eu te amo}}, {{Te ligo amanhã}} are what everyone says. With two verbs, the pronoun goes before the second one: {{Vou te ligar}}, {{Você pode me ajudar?}}
**Him, her, it, them.** Here everyday speech and careful writing really differ:

table: (the book) I'm going to buy it.

blocks.p: In conversation Brazilians say {{ele}}, {{ela}}, {{eles}}, {{elas}} after the verb, or, very often, nothing at all: {{Você quer o bolo? — Quero!}} The thing is clear, so it isn't said again. Teachers call {{vejo ela}} wrong in writing, where the forms are {{o, a, os, as}} before the verb, or {{-lo, -la}} after an infinitive (whose {{-r}} drops). Use the spoken forms when you talk, and recognise the written ones when you read.

**With me, for me.** After {{com}}: {{comigo}} “with me”, {{com você}} “with you”, {{com a gente}} or {{conosco}} “with us”. After other prepositions, “me” is {{mim}}: {{pra mim}} “for me”, {{de mim}} “of me”.

ex.tr: I love you.

ex.t: Você me ajuda com essa mala?
ex.tr: Will you help me with this suitcase?
I'm going to send you the address.
Carla? Yes, I know her.

ex.t: Você conhece esse livro? — Conheço. Adoro!
ex.tr: Do you know this book? — I do. I love it!
ex.note: no word for “it”: the thing is clear

Do you want to come with me?

“Me” as an object is {{me}}, before the verb; {{eu}} is only for the subject.
After a preposition, “me” is {{mim}}.

lessons.title: Say what you did
lessons.summary: Tell someone what you did yesterday or last week, and ask what they did: the past of regular verbs.
lessons.topic: The {{pretérito perfeito}} of regular verbs ({{falei, comi, abri}}); {{ontem}}, {{semana passada}}, {{há}} “ago”

goal.t: Ontem eu trabalhei até tarde e depois jantei com uma amiga.
goal.tr: Yesterday I worked late and then had dinner with a friend.

dialog.t: E aí, o que você fez ontem?
dialog.tr: So, what did you do yesterday?

dialog.t: Trabalhei o dia todo. E à noite assisti a um filme.
dialog.tr: I worked all day. And in the evening I watched a movie.

dialog.t: Qual filme?
dialog.tr: Which movie?

dialog.t: Um brasileiro. Gostei muito! E você?
dialog.tr: A Brazilian one. I liked it a lot! And you?

dialog.t: Eu estudei pra prova e dormi cedo.
dialog.tr: I studied for the test and went to bed early.

dialog.t: Coitada!
dialog.tr: Poor you!

blocks.means: the form of a verb that shows when something happens: I work (now), I worked (in the past).

blocks.p: **What happened, and is finished.** For actions that are over (yesterday, last week, in 2019), Portuguese uses the {{pretérito perfeito}}. Regular verbs follow three patterns:
The {{nós}} form is the same as in the present: {{falamos}} is “we speak” or “we spoke”, and the time words make it clear. ({{A gente falou}} avoids the question.)
**Spelling in the “I” form.** To keep their sound, verbs in {{-car}}, {{-gar}} and {{-çar}} change their last consonant: {{ficar}} → {{fiquei}}, {{chegar}} → {{cheguei}}, {{começar}} → {{comecei}}.

**When.** {{ontem}} yesterday, {{anteontem}} the day before yesterday, {{ontem à noite}} last night, {{semana passada}} last week, {{mês passado}}, {{ano passado}}. And “ago” is {{há}} + the time: {{há dois dias}} “two days ago” (lesson 30 says more).
**Questions and answers** work as always, with no helper word: {{Você gostou?}} “Did you like it?” — {{Gostei!}} / {{Não gostei.}}

ex.tr: I arrived last night.
Did you like the movie?
We ate really well.

ex.t: Ela morou dois anos no Japão.
ex.tr: She lived in Japan for two years.

ex.t: Eles abriram uma loja no centro.
ex.tr: They opened a store downtown.
I didn't sleep at all.

ex.t: Comprei esse vestido há uma semana.
ex.tr: I bought this dress a week ago.

blocks.tip: {{Gostei!}} “I liked it!” is how Brazilians say they enjoyed something they just tried: a meal, a show, a place.

mistakes.why: A finished action in the past: {{trabalhei}}.
{{Chegar}} keeps its hard g sound with a {{u}}: {{cheguei}}.

mistakes.tr: Did you eat? — Yes, I did.
mistakes.why: No helper verb in Portuguese, in the past either: answer with the verb.

lessons.title: Tell someone about your weekend
lessons.summary: Say where you went, what you did and how it was, with the irregular verbs you use most.
lessons.topic: Irregular perfeito: {{fui}} ({{ir}} and {{ser}}), {{tive, estive, fiz, pude, quis, disse, vi, vim, dei, trouxe}}; {{Como foi?}}

goal.t: No sábado eu fui à praia e fiz um churrasco com os amigos.
goal.tr: On Saturday I went to the beach and had a barbecue with friends.

dialog.t: E o fim de semana, como foi?

dialog.t: Foi ótimo! Fui a Petrópolis com meu namorado.
dialog.tr: It was great! I went to Petrópolis with my boyfriend.

dialog.t: Que legal! O que vocês fizeram?

dialog.t: A gente foi ao museu, fez uma trilha e trouxe chocolate pra todo mundo.
dialog.tr: We went to the museum, did a hike and brought chocolate for everyone.

dialog.t: E cadê o meu?

dialog.t: Ih… não deu!
dialog.tr: Oops… it didn't work out!

blocks.p: **The irregular ones.** The verbs you use most are irregular in the past. Look at the “I” and “he” forms first: they're the ones you'll say most often.
**{{ser}} and {{ir}} share one past.** {{Fui}} is both “I went” and “I was”: {{Fui ao Rio}} “I went to Rio”, {{Fui professor}} “I was a teacher”. The rest of the sentence tells you which.
**{{pôde}} or {{pode}}?** The hat tells them apart in writing: {{ele pode}} “he can”, {{ele pôde}} “he could, was able to”.
**How was it?** {{Como foi?}} — {{Foi ótimo!}}, {{Foi legal}}, {{Foi horrível}}.

ex.tr: How was the trip? — It was amazing!

Where have you been?

lessons.title: Say what you've done and haven't done yet
lessons.summary: Talk about your experiences and what you've done so far: “Have you ever been to Bahia?”, “Not yet!”.
lessons.topic: {{já}}, {{ainda não}}, {{nunca}} with the perfeito, where English says “have done”; {{uma vez}}, {{duas vezes}}

goal.t: Já comi feijoada, mas nunca experimentei açaí.
goal.tr: I've had feijoada, but I've never tried açaí.

dialog.t: Você já foi a Salvador?
dialog.tr: Have you ever been to Salvador?

dialog.t: Ainda não. Mas já fui ao Rio duas vezes.
dialog.tr: Not yet. But I've been to Rio twice.

dialog.t: E você já comeu acarajé?
dialog.tr: And have you ever eaten acarajé?

dialog.t: Nunca! O que é isso?
dialog.tr: Never! What's that?

dialog.t: É uma comida da Bahia. Você tem que experimentar!
dialog.tr: It's a food from Bahia. You have to try it!

dialog.t: Já anotei!
dialog.tr: I've already written it down!

blocks.p: **English “have done” → the plain past.** English says “I have eaten”, “Have you ever been…?” for experiences and for things done by now. Portuguese uses lesson 25's past, with a small word that gives the meaning:

table: Have you ever been to Rio?

blocks.p: **{{já}}** is “already” or “ever”: {{Você já…?}} asks “Have you (ever, already)…?”. Answer yes with {{Já!}} or the verb: {{Já fui.}}, {{Fui, sim.}}
**{{ainda não}}** “not yet” goes before the verb: {{Ainda não terminei}} “I haven't finished yet”.
**{{nunca}}** “never” goes before the verb, with no {{não}}: {{Nunca fui à Bahia.}} If it comes after the verb, put {{não}} before: {{Não fui nunca.}}
**How many times.** {{uma vez}} once, {{duas vezes}} twice, {{muitas vezes}} many times, {{várias vezes}} several times.

ex.t: Você já esteve em São Paulo?
ex.tr: Have you ever been to São Paulo?

ex.t: Já li esse livro duas vezes.
ex.tr: I've read this book twice.
I haven't had lunch yet.
I've never seen snow.
Has the bus left already?
I've already had coffee, thanks.

blocks.tip: Careful: {{tenho comido}} doesn't mean “I have eaten”. It means “I've been eating (lately)”, and lesson 45 shows it. For “I've eaten”, say {{Já comi}}.

mistakes.wrong: Eu tenho comido feijoada uma vez.
mistakes.right: Eu já comi feijoada uma vez.
mistakes.why: For an experience, use the plain past with {{já}}.
{{Nunca}} before the verb already says “never”: no {{não}}.

lessons.title: Describe how things used to be
lessons.summary: Describe your childhood and the old days: where you lived, what things were like, what you used to do.
lessons.topic: The imperfeito ({{morava, fazia, era, tinha, ia}}) for habits and descriptions; {{costumava}}; {{o senhor}}, {{a senhora}}

goal.t: Quando eu era criança, eu morava numa cidade pequena.
goal.tr: When I was a kid, I lived in a small town.

dialog.t: Na minha época, a gente não tinha celular.
dialog.tr: In my day, we didn't have cell phones.

dialog.t: E o que vocês faziam?

dialog.t: Ia, sim. A escola ficava longe, mas todo mundo ia junto.
dialog.tr: Yes, I did. The school was far, but everyone went together.

blocks.p: **A second past.** Lesson 25's past tells what happened and is over. Portuguese has another past, the {{imperfeito}}, for how things **were** and what **used to** happen: habits, descriptions, the background of a story.
**Easy forms.** {{-ar}} verbs take {{-ava}}; {{-er}} and {{-ir}} verbs take {{-ia}}. “I” and “he” are the same ({{eu morava}}, {{ele morava}}), and {{ir}} is {{ia}}. Only four verbs are irregular:

**What it's for.** Habits: {{Eu jogava futebol todo sábado}} “I used to play soccer every Saturday”. Descriptions: {{A casa era grande e tinha um jardim}} “The house was big and had a garden”. Age and the time: {{Eu tinha dez anos}}, {{Eram oito horas}}.
**“Used to”.** The imperfeito alone already means it. You'll also hear {{costumava}} + infinitive: {{Eu costumava acordar cedo}} “I used to get up early”.
**{{a senhora}}, {{o senhor}}.** The grandson says {{a senhora}} to his grandmother: it's the respectful “you” for older people and formal moments, with the same verb form as {{você}}.

ex.tr: I used to be very shy.

ex.t: A gente morava perto da praia.
ex.tr: We lived near the beach.
My grandfather had a farm.

ex.tr: Every summer we would go to my aunt's house.

ex.tr: What did you want to be when you were a kid?

blocks.tip: {{Tinha}} is also the past of {{tem}} “there is”: {{Tinha muita gente na festa}} “There were a lot of people at the party”.

lessons.title: Tell a story
lessons.summary: Set the scene and tell what happened: “I was sleeping when the phone rang.”
lessons.topic: Perfeito (events) and imperfeito (the scene) together; {{estava}} + {{-ndo}}; {{quando}}, {{enquanto}}, {{aí}}, {{de repente}}

goal.t: Eu estava dormindo quando o telefone tocou.
goal.tr: I was sleeping when the phone rang.

dialog.t: Você não vai acreditar no que aconteceu ontem!
dialog.tr: You won't believe what happened yesterday!

dialog.t: O quê?

dialog.t: Eu estava andando na praia, estava tudo tranquilo… e aí um macaco roubou o meu sanduíche!

dialog.t: Mentira! Onde você estava?

dialog.t: Em Ilhabela. Eu estava comendo e, de repente, ele pegou e saiu correndo!

dialog.t: Que história!

blocks.p: **The scene and the events.** A story needs both pasts. The imperfeito paints the scene, what **was going on**: the weather, where you were, what you were doing. The perfeito tells what **happened**, one event after another.

table: {{Dormi às nove.}} I went to bed at nine.
{{A gente estava jantando}} We were having dinner

blocks.p: **{{estava}} + {{-ndo}}.** Lesson 18's form, in the past: {{Eu estava dormindo}} “I was sleeping”. It's the usual way to set a scene that something interrupts: {{Eu estava dormindo quando o telefone tocou.}}

**{{quando}} and {{enquanto}}.** {{quando}} “when” often brings in the event: {{…quando o telefone tocou}}. {{enquanto}} “while” goes with the background: {{Enquanto eu cozinhava, ele arrumava a casa}} “While I cooked, he tidied the house”.
**Moving the story on.** {{primeiro}} first, {{depois}} then, afterwards, {{aí}} and then (very Brazilian, in speech), {{de repente}} suddenly, {{no fim}} in the end.

ex.t: Estava fazendo sol, então a gente foi à praia.
ex.tr: It was sunny, so we went to the beach.

ex.t: Quando eu cheguei, todo mundo estava dançando.
ex.tr: When I arrived, everyone was dancing.

ex.t: Eu estava no ônibus quando vi o acidente.
ex.tr: I was on the bus when I saw the accident.

ex.t: Enquanto ela trabalhava, eu cuidava das crianças.
ex.tr: While she was working, I looked after the kids.

ex.t: Aí ele olhou pra mim e começou a rir.
ex.tr: And then he looked at me and started laughing.
In the end, everything worked out.

blocks.tip: Brazilians love telling stories with {{aí}}: {{Aí eu falei… aí ele falou…}} “So I said… and then he said…”. Perfect in speech; in writing, use {{depois}} or {{então}}.

lessons.title: Say how long and how long ago
lessons.summary: Say how long you've lived, worked or studied somewhere, and when things happened: “for two years”, “two years ago”.
lessons.topic: {{há}} / {{faz}} + time with the present (“for”) and with the past (“ago”); {{desde}}; {{daqui a}}

goal.t: Moro no Brasil há dois anos.
goal.tr: I've lived in Brazil for two years.

dialog.t: Você mora aqui há muito tempo?
dialog.tr: Have you lived here long?

dialog.t: Não, só há seis meses. Cheguei em abril.
dialog.tr: No, only six months. I arrived in April.

dialog.t: E você estuda português há quanto tempo?

dialog.t: Faz um ano. Comecei antes de vir.
dialog.tr: For a year. I started before I came.

dialog.t: Você fala muito bem!

dialog.t: Obrigada! Mas ainda tenho muito que aprender.

blocks.p: **For how long: {{há}} + the present.** Where English says “I've lived here for two years”, Portuguese uses the **present**, because you still live there: {{Moro aqui há dois anos}}, literally “I live here, it has been two years”.
**Ago: {{há}} + the past.** With the perfeito, the same {{há}} means “ago”: {{Cheguei há dois anos}} “I arrived two years ago”.

table: I've lived here for two years.
How long have you lived here?

blocks.p: **{{faz}}: the same, in speech.** In conversation {{faz}} often takes the place of {{há}}: {{Moro aqui faz dois anos}}, or {{Faz dois anos que moro aqui}}. And {{Faz tempo!}} “It's been a while!”.

**{{há}} or {{a}}?** {{Há}}, with an h (it's the verb {{haver}}), is for time that has passed: {{há dois dias}}. Plain {{a}} is for the future and for distance: {{daqui a dois dias}} “in two days”, {{a dez minutos daqui}} “ten minutes from here”.
**{{desde}}** “since” takes a starting point: {{desde ontem}}, {{desde janeiro}}, {{desde criança}} “since I was a kid”.

blocks.tip: {{Há quanto tempo!}} “Long time no see!” is the classic greeting for an old friend you haven't seen in a while.

lessons.title: Compare things
lessons.summary: Say what's bigger, better, cheaper or the best: compare cities, prices, food and people.
lessons.topic: {{mais}} / {{menos}} … {{(do) que}}; {{tão}} … {{quanto}}; {{melhor, pior, maior, menor}}; {{o mais…}}; {{-íssimo}}

goal.t: São Paulo é maior que o Rio, mas o Rio é mais bonito.

dialog.t: Qual é melhor, o apartamento da Rua Augusta ou o da Vila Mariana?

blocks.p: **More, less.** Put {{mais}} “more” or {{menos}} “less” before the adjective, and {{(do) que}} “than” after: {{O Rio é mais bonito (do) que São Paulo.}} With or without {{do}}, both are right.
English adds “-er” to short words (bigger, cheaper); Portuguese always uses {{mais}}: {{mais barato}} “cheaper”, {{mais rápido}} “faster”.
**Four special ones.** Like “better” and “worse” in English, these don't take {{mais}}:

**The most.** {{o mais}}, {{a mais}} + adjective, and {{de}} for “in”: {{o restaurante mais caro da cidade}} “the most expensive restaurant in the city”. And {{o melhor}}, {{o pior}}, {{o maior}}, {{o menor}}.
**Very, very.** {{-íssimo}} adds a lot: {{caro}} → {{caríssimo}} “super expensive”, {{lindo}} → {{lindíssimo}}; and {{muito mais}} is “much more”: {{muito mais barato}} “much cheaper”.

ex.tr: She's as smart as her sister.

lessons.title: Sound friendly with little words
lessons.summary: Use the little endings Brazilians put everywhere: {{um cafezinho}}, {{rapidinho}}, {{um minutinho}}.
lessons.topic: Diminutives {{-inho}}, {{-zinho}}; augmentative {{-ão}}

goal.t: Espera um minutinho, já volto!

dialog.t: Bom dia, querida! O que vai ser hoje?
dialog.tr: Good morning, dear! What'll it be today?

dialog.tr: Good morning! A coffee and two bread rolls, please.

blocks.means: a form of a word that makes it smaller, or sound cuter or friendlier: doggie, sweetie.

blocks.p: **{{-inho}}, {{-inha}}.** Add it to a noun or an adjective and the thing becomes small, cute, or just friendlier. Words ending in {{-o}} or {{-a}} drop that vowel; words ending in a stressed vowel, a consonant or {{-ão}} add {{-zinho}}:

Spelling keeps the sound: {{-co}}, {{-ca}} become {{-qu-}} ({{pouco}} → {{pouquinho}}, {{fresco}} → {{fresquinho}}), {{-go}} becomes {{-gu-}} ({{amigo}} → {{amiguinho}}), and {{-ço}} becomes {{-c-}} ({{pedaço}} → {{pedacinho}}).

**Not always small.** Brazilians use the diminutive all day, mostly for warmth: {{um cafezinho}} is just “a coffee”, offered kindly; {{Espera um minutinho}} “Just a minute”; {{rapidinho}} “real quick”; {{devagarinho}} “nice and slow”. On adjectives and adverbs it often means “nicely” or “really”: {{fresquinho}} “nice and fresh”, {{pertinho}} “really close”, {{cedinho}} “nice and early”.
**The opposite: {{-ão}}.** {{-ão}} makes things big: {{casa}} → {{casarão}} “mansion”, {{carro}} → {{carrão}} “big car”, {{amigo}} → {{amigão}} “buddy”. {{Obrigadão!}} is a hearty “thanks a lot!”.

ex.tr: Shall we have a coffee?
Speak a little more slowly, please.
The bakery is really close to here.
What a cute little dog!
I'll be back real quick.
I bought a big car!

blocks.tip: Diminutives are friendly, but they can be ironic too: {{um probleminha}} “a little problem” can be a big one, said gently.

lessons.title: Give reasons and connect ideas
lessons.summary: Say why, give reasons and results, and join your ideas: because, so, but, if, while.
lessons.topic: {{por que}}, {{porque}}, {{por quê}}; {{mas}}, {{então}}, {{por isso}}, {{se}}, {{enquanto}}

goal.t: Não fui à festa porque estava muito cansado.
goal.tr: I didn't go to the party because I was really tired.

blocks.p: **Why? Because.** Four spellings, all said the same way, that you tell apart in writing:
**Linking words.** These join two ideas into one sentence:

table: {{Ele cozinha enquanto eu lavo a louça.}}

blocks.p: **{{então}} or {{por isso}}?** Both mean “so, that's why”. {{Por isso}} (literally “for that”) points more clearly at the reason: {{Estava cansado, por isso fui embora}} “I was tired; that's why I left”. {{Então}} is also a filler in speech, like English “so…”.

**{{se}} “if”** with the present, for real situations: {{Se você está com fome, tem pão na cozinha}} “If you're hungry, there's bread in the kitchen”. For the future and for imagining, Portuguese has special forms: lessons 40 and 41.

lessons.title: Say whose things are
lessons.summary: Ask whose something is, and say “Ana's car”, “his”, “hers” and “a friend of mine”.
lessons.topic: {{De quem é…?}}; {{o carro da Ana}}; {{dele, dela, deles}} for “his, her, their”; {{o meu}}; {{um amigo meu}}

goal.t: Esse carro é seu? — Não, é dela.
goal.tr: Is this car yours? — No, it's hers.

dialog.tr: Whose coat is this?

blocks.p: **Whose?: {{De quem…?}}** {{De quem é esse livro?}} “Whose book is this?” Answer: {{É meu}} “It's mine”, {{É da Ana}} “It's Ana's”.
**{{de}} + the owner.** Portuguese has no “'s”: it says “the car of Ana”, {{o carro da Ana}}; {{a casa do meu pai}} “my father's house”; {{o quarto das crianças}} “the children's room”.

**His, her, their: {{dele}}, {{dela}}, {{deles}}, {{delas}}.** {{Seu}} and {{sua}} can mean “your”, “his”, “her” and “their”, which gets confusing. So Brazilians keep {{seu}} for “your”, and for the others say “of him”, “of her” after the noun:
Notice the difference from {{meu}} and {{seu}}: {{dele}} and {{dela}} match the **owner** (a man, a woman), not the thing. {{A casa dele}} is “his house”; {{o carro dela}} “her car”.

**Mine, yours.** The same words, often with “the”: {{Esse é o meu}} “This one is mine”, {{A minha é azul}} “Mine is blue”. Right after {{é}}, no “the”: {{É meu}}, {{É dela}}. And “a friend of mine” is {{um amigo meu}}, “a cousin of hers” {{uma prima dela}}.

ex.tr: Whose backpack is this?

ex.t: É a casa da minha avó.
ex.tr: It's my grandmother's house.

ex.tr: Carla and her husband live in Recife.

ex.t: O Pedro esqueceu o celular dele aqui.
ex.tr: Pedro left his phone here.
Is this seat yours?
A friend of mine works there.

blocks.tip: {{Nossa!}} (“ours!”) is also Brazil's favorite word of surprise: {{Nossa, que lindo!}} “Wow, how beautiful!” It comes from {{Nossa Senhora}} “Our Lady”.

lessons.title: Say which one you mean
lessons.summary: Describe people, things and places with a whole sentence: “the friend who lives in Lisbon”, “the city where I was born”.
lessons.topic: {{que}} “who, which, that”, never left out; {{onde}} “where”; {{o que}} “what”; {{com quem}}, {{de que}}

goal.t: Conheci uma pessoa que fala cinco línguas!
goal.tr: I met someone who speaks five languages!

dialog.t: Quem é aquela menina que está falando com o Léo?
dialog.tr: Who's that girl who's talking to Léo?

dialog.t: É a Clara, a amiga que mora em Lisboa.
dialog.tr: That's Clara, the friend who lives in Lisbon.

dialog.t: Ah, a que trabalha com cinema?

dialog.t: Essa mesma. E aquele é o cara que fez o bolo.
dialog.tr: That's her. And that's the guy who made the cake.

dialog.t: O bolo que eu comi três vezes? Preciso conhecer ele!
dialog.tr: The cake I had three times? I need to meet him!

blocks.p: **{{que}}: who, which, that.** One word joins a description to a noun, for people and for things: {{a amiga que mora em Lisboa}} “the friend who lives in Lisbon”, {{o bolo que eu comi}} “the cake (that) I ate”.
Unlike English, Portuguese never leaves it out: “the cake I ate” must be {{o bolo que eu comi}}.
**{{onde}}: where.** For places: {{a cidade onde eu nasci}} “the city where I was born”, {{o bar onde a gente se conheceu}} “the bar where we met”.
**{{o que}}: what (“the thing that”).** {{Não entendi o que você disse}} “I didn't understand what you said”, {{Isso é o que eu quero}} “That's what I want”.

**With a preposition.** When the verb needs one ({{falar com}}, {{precisar de}}), it goes before {{que}}, or before {{quem}} for people: {{a pessoa com quem eu falei}} “the person I talked to”, {{o livro de que eu preciso}} “the book I need”. In relaxed speech many Brazilians drop it ({{o livro que eu preciso}}); you'll hear both.
**The one who.** {{a que trabalha com cinema}} “the one (a woman) who works in film”, {{os que chegaram cedo}} “the ones who arrived early”.

ex.t: Conheci uma pessoa que fala cinco línguas!
ex.tr: I met someone who speaks five languages!

ex.tr: The movie we saw yesterday was great.

ex.tr: I didn't understand what he said.

ex.tr: The guy I talked to was very nice.

ex.t: Tudo que eu quero é dormir.
ex.tr: All I want is to sleep.

blocks.tip: {{Conhecer}} in the past, {{conheci}}, is how you say “I met” someone: {{Conheci minha esposa em 2015}} “I met my wife in 2015”.

lessons.title: Say how something made you feel
lessons.summary: Say you got happy, nervous or scared, that you stayed home, or that something looks good on someone: the many jobs of {{ficar}}.
lessons.topic: {{ficar}}: become ({{fiquei feliz}}), stay ({{fiquei em casa}}), be located, keep, suit; {{Fica tranquilo!}}

goal.t: Fiquei muito feliz com a notícia!
goal.tr: I was really happy about the news!

dialog.t: Você soube? A Lu passou no vestibular!
dialog.tr: Did you hear? Lu passed the university entrance exam!

dialog.t: Sério? Que demais! Ela deve estar muito feliz.
dialog.tr: Really? That's awesome! She must be very happy.

dialog.t: Ficou! Ela chorou de alegria.
dialog.tr: She was! She cried with joy.

dialog.t: E você, ficou nervosa esperando o resultado?
dialog.tr: And you, did you get nervous waiting for the result?

dialog.t: Fiquei! Mas agora vou fazer um bolo pra comemorar.

blocks.p: **{{ficar}}: one verb, many jobs.** You know it for where places are ({{Onde fica o banco?}}). Here are its other everyday meanings:

table: I got happy, I was happy (about it).
This shirt looks good on you.

blocks.p: **Become: {{ficar}} + adjective.** English says “get angry”, “be happy about something”. Portuguese uses {{ficar}} for a feeling that starts because something happens: {{Fiquei triste quando ele foi embora}} “I got sad when he left”. Compare: {{Estou feliz}} “I'm happy (now)”; {{Fiquei feliz}} “I became happy (when it happened)”.
Common ones: {{ficar nervoso}} get nervous, {{ficar bravo}} get angry, {{ficar com medo}} get scared, {{ficar doente}} get sick, {{ficar pronto}} get ready, {{ficar sabendo}} find out.
**As a command.** {{Fica tranquilo!}} “Don't worry!”, {{Fica à vontade}} “Make yourself at home”, {{Fica pra jantar!}} “Stay for dinner!”.

ex.tr: He got angry with me.
I got scared of the dog.

ex.t: A gente ficou no hotel do lado da praia.
ex.tr: We stayed at the hotel next to the beach.
When will it be ready?

ex.t: Essa cor fica ótima em você!
ex.tr: That color looks great on you!
Make yourself at home!

blocks.tip: In Brazilian slang, {{ficar}} with a person means to kiss or make out without dating: {{Eles ficaram na festa}}. So be careful how you say {{Fiquei com ela}}!

mistakes.tr: I was happy when I won.
mistakes.why: A feeling that starts because something happens: {{ficar}}.

lessons.title: Ask politely
lessons.summary: Make polite requests at a hotel, a restaurant or on the phone: “I'd like…”, “Could you…?”, “Would it be possible…?”.
lessons.topic: The conditional ({{gostaria, poderia, seria}}); {{queria}} and {{ia}} for “would” in speech; three levels of polite

goal.t: Eu gostaria de reservar uma mesa para quatro, por favor.
goal.tr: I'd like to reserve a table for four, please.

dialog.t: Restaurante Sabor da Terra, boa noite.
dialog.tr: Sabor da Terra restaurant, good evening.

dialog.t: Boa noite! Eu gostaria de reservar uma mesa para sábado.
dialog.tr: Good evening! I'd like to reserve a table for Saturday.

dialog.t: Pois não. Para quantas pessoas?
dialog.tr: Certainly. For how many people?

dialog.t: Quatro. Seria possível às oito?
dialog.tr: Four. Would eight o'clock be possible?

dialog.t: Às oito está cheio. Poderia ser às nove?

dialog.t: Pode ser, sim. Obrigado!
dialog.tr: That works, yes. Thanks!

blocks.means: the form of a verb for what would happen, and for being polite: I would like, could you…?

blocks.p: **Softer requests.** Portuguese makes “would” with the infinitive plus {{-ia}}. It sounds polite and a little formal: it's what you use on the phone, at a hotel, with a stranger.

The endings are the same for every verb: {{eu gostaria}}, {{você gostaria}}, {{nós gostaríamos}}, {{eles gostariam}}. Only three are irregular: {{fazer}} → {{faria}}, {{dizer}} → {{diria}}, {{trazer}} → {{traria}}.
**Three levels of polite.** From plain to formal:

{{Queria}}, from lesson 4, is a past form used as a soft “I'd like”. In speech, Brazilians often use this kind of past for “would” in general: {{Eu ia adorar}} “I'd love it”, instead of {{Eu adoraria}}.
**Asking politely.** {{Você poderia…?}} “Could you…?”, {{Seria possível…?}} “Would it be possible…?”, {{Você se importa de…?}} “Do you mind…?”, {{Por gentileza}} “Kindly” (very polite).

ex.t: Você poderia me ajudar com as malas?
ex.tr: Could you help me with the suitcases?
Would it be possible to change rooms?

ex.t: Gostaria de falar com o gerente.
ex.tr: I'd like to speak with the manager.

ex.t: Por gentileza, onde fica o banheiro?
ex.tr: Excuse me, could you tell me where the restroom is?
I'd do that with pleasure.

ex.t: Eu ia adorar ir com vocês!
ex.tr: I'd love to go with you!

blocks.tip: {{Pode ser}} (“it can be”) is the easy way to accept a suggestion: {{Às nove? — Pode ser!}} “At nine? — Sure, that works!”

mistakes.why: {{Gostar}} always takes {{de}}, in the conditional too.
{{Poder}} takes the infinitive directly.
{{Fazer}} is irregular: {{faria}}.

lessons.title: Say what you want someone else to do
lessons.summary: Ask, want and hope that other people do things: “I want you to come”, “I hope you like it”.
lessons.topic: The present subjunctive after {{querer que}}, {{pedir que}}, {{esperar que}}, {{tomara que}}; the same person: the infinitive

goal.t: Quero que você venha à minha festa!
goal.tr: I want you to come to my party!

dialog.t: Amanhã é meu aniversário. Quero que você venha!
dialog.tr: Tomorrow is my birthday. I want you to come!

dialog.t: Claro que vou! Quer que eu leve alguma coisa?
dialog.tr: Of course I'll come! Do you want me to bring anything?

dialog.t: Não precisa. Só peço que você chegue cedo.
dialog.tr: No need. I only ask that you get there early.

dialog.t: Pode deixar. Espero que faça sol!
dialog.tr: Leave it to me. I hope it's sunny!

dialog.t: Tomara que sim! A festa é no quintal.
dialog.tr: Let's hope so! The party's in the backyard.

blocks.means: a set of verb forms for things that aren't facts yet: wishes, requests, doubts, possibilities. English keeps a trace of it: “I suggest that he **be** on time.”

blocks.p: **One person wants another to do something.** English says “I want you to come”. Portuguese says “I want that you come”, and the second verb takes a special form, the present subjunctive: {{Quero que você venha.}}

**You already know its form**: it's the written command of lesson 23. Take the “I” form of the present, drop the {{-o}}, and add the opposite vowel: {{-ar}} verbs get {{-e}}, {{-er}} and {{-ir}} verbs get {{-a}}.
Six common verbs don't follow the rule: {{ser}} → {{seja}}, {{estar}} → {{esteja}}, {{ir}} → {{vá}}, {{dar}} → {{dê}}, {{saber}} → {{saiba}}, {{querer}} → {{queira}}.
**When: after a wish or a request about someone else.**

table: I ask you to arrive early.
I hope it all works out.

blocks.p: {{Tomara que}} (“may it be that”) is a very Brazilian “I hope”: {{Tomara!}} alone, or {{Tomara que sim}} “Let's hope so”.
**The same person? The infinitive.** If the one who wants and the one who does are the same, no {{que}}: {{Quero ir}} “I want to go”; {{Quero que você vá}} “I want you to go”.

**A shortcut in speech.** To ask someone to do something, Brazilians often say {{pedir pra}} + infinitive: {{Ela pediu pra eu chegar cedo}} “She asked me to arrive early”. It's perfectly normal, and it avoids the subjunctive.

ex.t: Quero que vocês conheçam a minha família.
ex.tr: I want you to meet my family.
I hope you like it!
Let's hope it doesn't rain tomorrow.

ex.t: Meu chefe quer que eu viaje na segunda.

ex.tr: Do you want me to help you?

mistakes.why: Wanting someone else to do something: {{que}} + the subjunctive.
After {{espero que}}, the subjunctive: {{goste}}.
The same person wants and does: just the infinitive.

lessons.title: Give advice and doubt things
lessons.summary: Tell someone what's best for them, say what you think and what you doubt, and say “maybe”.
lessons.topic: {{é melhor que}}, {{é importante que}} + subjunctive; {{acho que}} (normal verb) vs {{não acho que}}, {{duvido que}} (subjunctive); {{talvez}}

goal.t: É melhor você levar um guarda-chuva. Acho que vai chover.
goal.tr: You'd better take an umbrella. I think it's going to rain.

dialog.t: Estou pensando em comprar um carro.
dialog.tr: I'm thinking of buying a car.

dialog.t: Sério? Em São Paulo? Não acho que seja uma boa ideia.
dialog.tr: Really? In São Paulo? I don't think it's a good idea.

dialog.t: Por quê?
dialog.tr: Why?

dialog.t: O trânsito é horrível. É melhor que você use o metrô.
dialog.tr: The traffic is terrible. You'd better use the subway.

dialog.t: Talvez você tenha razão.
dialog.tr: Maybe you're right.

dialog.t: É importante que você pense bem antes.
dialog.tr: It's important that you think it over first.

blocks.p: **Advice: {{é melhor}}, {{é importante}}, {{é bom}} + {{que}} + subjunctive.** When you say what's best for someone to do, the verb after {{que}} is in the subjunctive, as in lesson 38:

table: It's important that you arrive early.

blocks.p: In everyday speech there's a shortcut: {{é melhor}} + the person + infinitive. {{É melhor você descansar}} “You'd better rest”, {{É melhor a gente ir}} “We'd better go”.

**Opinions: {{acho que}} or {{não acho que}}?** {{Acho que}} “I think that” states what you believe, so the verb after it is the normal one: {{Acho que ele está certo.}} When you doubt, the subjunctive comes in: {{Não acho que ele esteja certo}} “I don't think he's right”, {{Duvido que ele venha}} “I doubt he'll come”.

table: {{Não é verdade que ele more aqui.}}

blocks.p: In relaxed conversation many Brazilians say {{Não acho que é}} too; the subjunctive sounds more careful.

**Maybe: {{talvez}}.** Before the verb, {{talvez}} takes the subjunctive: {{Talvez ele esteja em casa}} “Maybe he's at home”, {{Talvez eu vá}} “Maybe I'll go”. And the short answers: {{Acho que sim}} “I think so”, {{Acho que não}} “I don't think so”.

ex.t: É melhor a gente sair cedo por causa do trânsito.
ex.tr: We'd better leave early because of the traffic.

ex.t: É importante que você beba muita água.
ex.tr: It's important that you drink a lot of water.
I think you're right.

ex.t: Não acho que seja tão difícil.
ex.tr: I don't think it's that hard.

lessons.title: Talk about when and if things happen
lessons.summary: Talk about the future with “when”, “if” and “as soon as”: “When I arrive, I'll call you.”
lessons.topic: The future subjunctive after {{quando}}, {{se}}, {{assim que}}: {{chegar}}, {{for}}, {{tiver}}, {{quiser}}, {{puder}}

goal.t: Quando eu chegar, te mando uma mensagem.
goal.tr: When I arrive, I'll send you a message.

blocks.p: **English uses the present; Portuguese has a future form.** “When I **arrive**, I'll call you”: after “when” and “if”, English uses the present. Portuguese uses a special form, the future subjunctive: {{Quando eu chegar, te ligo.}}

**The form.** For regular verbs it looks just like the infinitive: {{chegar}}, {{comer}}, {{abrir}}. The plural adds {{-mos}} and {{-em}}: {{quando nós chegarmos}}, {{quando eles chegarem}}. For irregular verbs, take the {{eles}} form of the perfeito (lesson 26) and drop {{-am}}: {{fizeram}} → {{fizer}}, {{tiveram}} → {{tiver}}.
Yes, {{vir}} is both the infinitive “to come” and the form of {{ver}} “see” here: {{quando eu vir}} “when I see”. In speech many Brazilians say {{quando eu ver}}, but {{vir}} is the correct one.
**When to use it.** After {{quando}} “when”, {{se}} “if”, {{assim que}} “as soon as”, {{depois que}} “after”, {{enquanto}} “while”, and after {{o que}} and {{quem}} about the future:

table: As soon as I know, I'll let you know.

blocks.p: The other half of the sentence is the plain present, {{vou}} + verb, or a command: {{Se chover, vou ficar em casa}} “If it rains, I'll stay home”.

ex.tr: If you want, I'll pick you up at the airport.
