ex.tr: If I have time tomorrow, I'll go to the beach.

blocks.tip: {{Se Deus quiser}} (“if God wants”) follows plans and hopes everywhere in Brazil: {{Ano que vem eu me formo, se Deus quiser.}} “I graduate next year, God willing.”

blocks.p: **Imagining.** For things that aren't true, or probably won't be, Portuguese puts two forms together: {{se}} + the past subjunctive, then the conditional of lesson 37. {{Se eu tivesse dinheiro, eu viajaria.}} “If I had money, I would travel.”
**The past subjunctive.** Take the {{eles}} form of the perfeito once more, drop {{-ram}}, and add {{-sse}}:
The plural forms: {{se nós falássemos}}, {{se eles falassem}}.

**“Would”: two ways.** The conditional ({{viajaria}}) is the careful form. In conversation Brazilians very often use the imperfeito instead, especially {{ia}} + infinitive: {{Se eu tivesse dinheiro, eu ia viajar}}, or even {{eu viajava}}. All three are common.

**Advice: {{Se eu fosse você…}}** “If I were you…”: {{Se eu fosse você, eu aceitava}} “If I were you, I'd accept”. **Wishes: {{Eu queria que…}}** + the past subjunctive: {{Eu queria que você estivesse aqui}} “I wish you were here”.

ex.tr: If I spoke Portuguese well, I'd live in Brazil.

ex.tr: What would you do in my place?

ex.tr: If I were you, I wouldn't go.

ex.t: Se fosse mais barato, eu comprava.

lessons.title: Wonder aloud and understand the news
lessons.summary: Wonder about things the Brazilian way, {{Será que…?}}, and understand the one-word future of the news and announcements.
lessons.topic: {{Será que…?}}; {{sei lá}}; the simple future ({{falarei, será, farei}}) to recognise

goal.t: Será que vai chover amanhã?

blocks.p: **Wondering aloud: {{Será que…?}}** Brazilians put {{será que}} (“will it be that…?”) in front of a question when they're wondering, or asking someone's opinion: {{Será que ela gostou?}} “Do you think she liked it?”, {{Será que vai chover?}} “I wonder if it'll rain”. It softens any question, and you'll hear it all day.
The answer is often {{Acho que sim}}, {{Acho que não}}, {{Sei lá}} “Who knows”, or a guess with {{deve}} (lesson 21): {{Deve estar dormindo}} “He must be asleep”.

**The one-word future.** {{Será}} is the future of {{ser}}. Portuguese has a future tense of its own: the infinitive plus endings. In conversation Brazilians use {{vou}} + verb instead (lesson 19); the one-word future lives in writing, the news, announcements and formal speech. Learn to recognise it:
Only three verbs are irregular: {{fazer}} → {{farei}}, {{dizer}} → {{direi}}, {{trazer}} → {{trarei}}. All the others just add the endings to the infinitive: {{será}}, {{terá}}, {{irá}}, {{poderá}}.
**Where you'll meet it.** Weather reports ({{Amanhã fará calor}}), the news ({{O presidente viajará na segunda}}), airports ({{O voo partirá às 22h}}), contracts and signs.

blocks.p: **Said that: {{disse que}}, {{falou que}}.** To pass on what someone said, use {{dizer}} or, in everyday speech, {{falar}}, then {{que}}: {{Ela disse que estava cansada}} “She said she was tired”. Portuguese never drops this {{que}}.
**The verb moves back in time**, as in English: the present becomes the imperfeito, and {{vou}} becomes {{ia}}:
A past stays as it is (or becomes {{tinha ido}}: lesson 44). If something is still true, you can keep the present: {{Ele disse que mora aqui}} (he still does).

**Asked if: {{perguntou se}}.** A yes/no question is passed on with {{se}} “if, whether”: {{Ele perguntou se você vem}} “He asked if you're coming”. A question with a question word keeps it: {{Ela perguntou onde você mora}}.

**Asked someone to: {{pediu pra}}** + infinitive (lesson 38): {{Ele pediu pra você ligar}} “He asked you to call”. **Tell someone: {{falar pra}}**: {{Fala pra ela que eu liguei}} “Tell her I called”. ({{Contar}} is “tell” a story or news: {{Me conta!}} “Tell me!”.)

lessons.topic: {{tinha}} + past participle; regular ({{falado, comido}}) and irregular participles ({{feito, dito, visto, aberto, escrito}})

goal.t: Quando eu cheguei, o filme já tinha começado.
goal.tr: When I arrived, the movie had already started.

dialog.t: Você chegou a tempo pro show?

blocks.means: the form of a verb used after “have” and to describe a result: (had) eaten, (is) closed, (was) made.

blocks.p: **The past before the past.** When you're telling a story in the past and need to go further back, use {{tinha}} + the past participle: {{O filme já tinha começado}} “The movie had already started” (before I arrived). It's English “had done”.
**The participle.** Regular verbs: {{-ar}} → {{-ado}}, {{-er}} and {{-ir}} → {{-ido}}: {{falado}}, {{comido}}, {{saído}}. Only {{tinha}} changes for the person:
Some common verbs have irregular participles:
**With {{já}} and {{nunca}}**, as in lesson 27: {{Eu nunca tinha visto o mar}} “I had never seen the sea”, {{Ela já tinha ido embora}} “She had already left”.

**Also a describing word.** A participle works as an adjective, matching its noun: {{a porta aberta}} “the open door”, {{um bolo feito em casa}} “a homemade cake”. Lesson 46 uses it for results: {{A loja está fechada.}}

goal.t: Tenho trabalhado muito ultimamente.
goal.tr: I've been working a lot lately.

dialog.t: Nossa, quanto tempo! Por onde você tem andado?
dialog.tr: Wow, long time! Where have you been?

dialog.t: Pois é! Tenho trabalhado demais. E à noite tenho estudado português.

blocks.p: **{{ter}} + participle: lately, again and again.** {{Tenho trabalhado}} means “I've been working (lately, repeatedly, up to now)”. It's for something that has been happening over a recent stretch of time and is still going on.
**Not the English present perfect.** This is the trap: “I have eaten” is **not** {{tenho comido}}. Compare:

table: I've been eating a lot lately.

blocks.p: It often comes with {{ultimamente}} “lately”, {{esses dias}} “these days”, {{nos últimos meses}} “in the last few months”.

lessons.title: Say how things are done and made
lessons.summary: Say when something was built and by whom, read signs like “For rent”, and ask “How do you make…?”.
lessons.topic: The passive: {{ser}} + participle ({{foi construída}}); {{se}} ({{aluga-se}}, {{como se faz}}); {{estar}} + participle for the result ({{está fechado}})

goal.t: O pão de queijo é feito com polvilho e queijo.
goal.tr: Cheese bread is made with tapioca flour and cheese.

dialog.t: Esta igreja foi construída em 1750.
dialog.tr: This church was built in 1750.

dialog.t: Nossa! E ainda está aberta?
dialog.tr: Wow! And is it still open?

dialog.t: Está, mas só aos domingos. Aqui não se pode tirar foto com flash.
dialog.tr: It is, but only on Sundays. You can't take flash photos here.

dialog.t: Entendi. E aquelas pinturas foram feitas por quem?
dialog.tr: Got it. And who were those paintings made by?

dialog.t: Foram pintadas por um artista da região.
dialog.tr: They were painted by an artist from the region.

blocks.means: a sentence where the thing acted on comes first, and whoever did it comes after “by”, or not at all: The church was built in 1750.

blocks.p: **{{ser}} + participle: the passive.** To say what happened to something, rather than who did it, use {{ser}} and the past participle of lesson 44. The participle matches its noun like an adjective: {{A igreja foi construída em 1750}}, {{Os quadros foram pintados por um artista local}}. “By” is {{por}}, which joins “the”: {{pelo}}, {{pela}}.
You'll meet it mostly in the news, in history and in writing: {{O suspeito foi preso}} “The suspect was arrested”, {{O livro foi traduzido para vinte línguas}}.

**{{se}}: the everyday way.** In speech and on signs, Portuguese often uses {{se}} instead, with no one mentioned: {{Aluga-se}} “For rent”, {{Vende-se}} “For sale”, {{Aqui se fala inglês}} “English spoken here”, {{Não se pode fumar}} “No smoking”. And the questions every learner needs: {{Como se diz…?}}, {{Como se faz…?}} “How do you make…?”.

**{{estar}} + participle: the result.** {{Ser}} tells the action; {{estar}} the state it left behind. {{A loja foi fechada às seis}} “The store was closed at six (someone closed it)”; {{A loja está fechada}} “The store is closed (now)”. The {{ser}} and {{estar}} of lesson 2, one more time.

ex.t: Essa casa foi construída pelo meu avô.
ex.tr: This house was built by my grandfather.
The restaurant is closed today.

ex.t: Os ingressos foram vendidos em uma hora.
ex.tr: The tickets were sold in an hour.
Waiter wanted.
Dinner's ready!

lessons.title: Give your opinion and disagree politely
lessons.summary: Say what you think, agree, disagree gently, and weigh both sides: “Although Rio is beautiful, it's expensive.”
lessons.topic: {{na minha opinião}}, {{pra mim}}, {{concordo}}; {{embora}} + subjunctive; {{apesar de}}; {{por um lado… por outro}}

goal.t: Na minha opinião, o Brasil tem a melhor comida do mundo.
goal.tr: In my opinion, Brazil has the best food in the world.

dialog.t: Pra mim, o melhor lugar pra morar é o Rio.
dialog.tr: For me, the best place to live is Rio.

dialog.t: Será? Eu discordo. Embora o Rio seja lindo, a vida lá é muito cara.
dialog.tr: Really? I disagree. Although Rio is beautiful, life there is very expensive.

dialog.t: Concordo que é caro, mas a qualidade de vida compensa.
dialog.tr: I agree it's expensive, but the quality of life makes up for it.

dialog.t: Depende. Por um lado, tem praia; por outro, tem muito trânsito.
dialog.tr: It depends. On the one hand, there's the beach; on the other, there's a lot of traffic.

dialog.t: É verdade. Mas mesmo assim eu prefiro o Rio!
dialog.tr: That's true. But even so, I prefer Rio!

dialog.t: Tá bom, cada um com a sua opinião.
dialog.tr: OK, to each their own.

blocks.p: **Giving an opinion.** {{Acho que…}} (lesson 39) is the most common. Others: {{Na minha opinião…}} “In my opinion…”, {{Pra mim…}} “For me…”, {{Eu acredito que…}} “I believe that…”, {{Tenho certeza de que…}} “I'm sure that…”.

**Agreeing and disagreeing.** {{Concordo}} “I agree”, {{Com certeza!}} “Definitely!”, {{É verdade}} “That's true”. Brazilians rarely disagree head-on: they soften it with {{Não sei, não…}}, {{Depende}}, {{Será?}}, {{Não concordo muito}} “I don't really agree”.

table: It depends. I don't really agree.
On the one hand… on the other…

blocks.p: **Although: {{embora}} + subjunctive.** {{Embora}} always takes the subjunctive: {{Embora seja caro, vale a pena}} “Although it's expensive, it's worth it”. In speech, {{apesar de}} + infinitive (or + a noun) is easier: {{Apesar de ser caro…}}, {{Apesar da chuva…}} “Despite the rain…”. And {{mesmo assim}} is “even so”.

table: {{Embora o Rio seja lindo, é caro.}}
{{Apesar de ser lindo, o Rio é caro.}}
{{O Rio é caro, mas mesmo assim eu adoro.}}

ex.t: Apesar da chuva, a viagem foi ótima.
ex.tr: Despite the rain, the trip was great.

lessons.title: Keep a conversation going
lessons.summary: React, ask for agreement and keep people talking with the little words that make you sound Brazilian: {{né?}}, {{sabe?}}, {{pois é}}, {{nossa!}}
lessons.topic: {{né?}}, {{sabe?}}, {{então}}, {{tipo}}, {{pois é}}, {{nossa!}}, {{sério?}}, {{e aí?}}; reactions and follow-up questions

goal.t: Sério? E aí, o que aconteceu depois?
goal.tr: Really? So what happened next?

dialog.t: Então, sabe aquele restaurante novo? Fui lá ontem.
dialog.tr: So, you know that new restaurant? I went there yesterday.

dialog.t: Ah, é? E aí, gostou?
dialog.tr: Oh yeah? So, did you like it?

dialog.t: Nossa, adorei! A comida é tipo… perfeita.
dialog.tr: Wow, I loved it! The food is like… perfect.

dialog.t: Sério? Mas não é caro?
dialog.tr: Really? But isn't it expensive?

dialog.t: Pois é, é um pouco. Mas vale a pena, sabe?
dialog.tr: Yeah, it is a bit. But it's worth it, you know?

dialog.t: Que legal! Vamos juntos um dia desses?
dialog.tr: How cool! Shall we go together one of these days?

blocks.p: **Little words that keep things moving.** Brazilian conversation is full of short words that show you're listening, ask for agreement, or give you time to think. They don't change the meaning, but without them you sound like a textbook.

table: “so…”: to start or to move on
“like”: before an example or a guess

blocks.p: **Showing interest.** React first: {{Que legal!}} “How cool!”, {{Que pena!}} “What a pity!”, {{Que chato!}} “How annoying!”. Then ask more, to keep the other person talking: {{E depois?}} “And then?”, {{Como assim?}} “What do you mean?”, {{E você gostou?}}

**Asking for agreement: {{né?}}** It's Brazil's tag question for everything: {{Você é americano, né?}} “You're American, aren't you?”, {{Vai chover, né?}} “It's going to rain, isn't it?”. The answer, as always since lesson 3, is the verb: {{Sou.}}, {{Vai.}}
**Gaining time.** {{Então…}}, {{Bom…}}, {{Deixa eu ver…}} “Let me see…”, {{Como é que se diz…?}} “How do you say…?”.

ex.t: Você é de São Paulo, né?
ex.tr: You're from São Paulo, aren't you?

ex.t: Pois é, a vida está corrida.
ex.tr: Yeah, life's hectic.
What do you mean? I didn't get it.

ex.t: Então, deixa eu ver… acho que sim.
ex.tr: So, let me see… I think so.

ex.t: Nossa, que chato! E aí, o que você fez?
ex.tr: Wow, how annoying! So what did you do?
Thank you! — Don't mention it!

blocks.tip: {{Imagina!}} (“imagine!”) is a warm Brazilian “You're welcome!” or “No trouble at all!”.
